strengths: The paper presents a coherent autoregressive visual-generation system built around an LLM-style backbone, with clearly motivated modifications for spatiotemporal data.
MM-RoPE is a simple, computationally inexpensive design, and the controlled validation-loss studies support the usefulness of distributed frequency allocation and position scaling.

AR-DF addresses a plausible shortcut in video masked modeling: temporally independent masks allow reconstruction from the same spatial location in neighboring frames. The proposed tube masking and partial-history inference policy are intuitive and practically relevant.

The system is evaluated across text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation, with competitive headline GenEval and VBench results despite relatively modest model size and reported training hardware. The paper also provides algorithms, architectural configurations, latency measurements, qualitative results, limitations, and a responsible-use discussion.
weaknesses: The main methodological claims are not validated with sufficiently strong generation-level ablations. MM-RoPE is evaluated primarily through validation cross-entropy on a 0.5B toy model, without showing its effect on GenEval, VBench, or human preference. Similarly, tube masking is compared with random masking using frame-wise loss curves, but the paper does not report final video metrics for the competing training schemes. Consequently, it remains unclear how much either contribution explains the headline system performance.

Benchmark comparability is problematic. GenEval prompts are rewritten with Qwen-32B specifically for Lumos-1, but no equivalent evaluation of baselines under the same rewriting procedure is reported. Video comparisons mix model sizes, training sets, resolutions, and auxiliary encoders, while only selected VBench dimensions are shown. There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, human evaluations, or sufficiently broad motion/temporal-quality evaluations.

The training data are described only as a curated collection of 60M images and 10M videos. Sources, licenses, filtering, deduplication, train-test contamination checks, captioning details, and data composition are omitted. This materially limits reproducibility and makes the benchmark and societal-risk assessment difficult to audit.

The claimed unified-model perspective is overstated. The implementation explicitly removes the language next-token loss, is trained from scratch, and evaluates neither language generation nor multimodal understanding. Preserving textual RoPE alone does not demonstrate preservation of language capabilities or readiness as a unified foundation model.

Important methodological details are ambiguous. The paper states that cross-entropy is computed only on 'unmasked' tokens even though the surrounding formulation suggests masked-token prediction; taken literally, this would permit trivial copying. The exact loss definition, sampling details, training schedules, number of optimization steps, hardware time, and dataset mixture probabilities are not fully specified.

The argument that an individual RoPE frequency becomes unusable after one period is technically oversimplified: RoPE positions are represented jointly across multiple frequencies, so periodicity in one channel does not by itself imply positional ambiguity. The proposed frequency redistribution may work empirically, but the theoretical motivation is weaker than presented.

Qualitative evidence for video generation consists of sparse sampled frames, which cannot substantiate claims about smooth motion, temporal coherence, or physical plausibility. Overall, the ideas and system results are promising, but the evidence supporting the central contributions is insufficient for a top-tier acceptance in the present form.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: efficient autoregressive video generation using an architecture close to standard LLMs, without a large external text encoder.

MM-RoPE and AR-DF are intuitive, practically motivated modifications. The discussion of frequency allocation in 3D RoPE and information leakage across video frames offers useful empirical observations.
The model is evaluated across text-to-image, text-to-video, and image-to-video tasks, with competitive GenEval and VBench results given its reported model size and training-data scale.
The paper provides algorithms, architecture configurations, inference-time measurements, several design sweeps, qualitative examples, and a discussion of societal risks.
weaknesses: The main methodological evidence is inadequate. MM-RoPE is evaluated primarily through validation-loss curves on a 0.5B model, without showing how its variants affect standard generation metrics. AR-DF is supported mainly by frame-wise losses, two selected VBench dimensions, and qualitative examples. Thus, the experiments do not establish that either proposed component causes the headline benchmark performance.

The novelty is limited and insufficiently differentiated from prior work. MM-RoPE largely rearranges coordinate assignments across RoPE frequency channels and empirically rescales positions, while AR-DF combines temporal tube masking, causal frame generation, and MaskGIT-style iterative decoding. Comparisons against the closest positional-encoding, diffusion-forcing, and autoregressive masking alternatives are not comprehensive.

The theoretical motivation for MM-RoPE is questionable. The claim that a sinusoidal channel should not exceed one period to avoid ambiguity overlooks how RoPE uses multiple frequencies jointly. No formal analysis demonstrates that the proposed interleaving improves positional distinguishability or explains why scaling latent coordinates by tokenizer compression ratios is principled.

The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled. Most baseline numbers appear imported from prior reports despite differences in data, resolution, parameter accounting, tokenizers, inference budgets, and prompt processing. Lumos-1 uniquely rewrites GenEval prompts using Qwen-32B, making the comparison especially difficult to interpret.

Video evaluation relies heavily on VBench and selected qualitative frames. There is no human evaluation, uncertainty analysis, evaluation over multiple random seeds, or convincing measurement of temporal artifacts and physical plausibility. Reporting only partial VBench dimensions further limits scrutiny.

Reproducibility is poor. The 60M-image and 10M-video datasets are not identified or documented; their sources, licenses, filtering, deduplication, and possible benchmark contamination are unknown. Training duration, total compute, random seeds, sampling details, and several data-processing choices are also missing. The abstract's code-and-model availability statement contains no usable link.

There is an important ambiguity in the training objective: the text states that cross-entropy is computed only on the unmasked tokens, although masked-token prediction would ordinarily optimize masked positions. The loss in Algorithm 1 is not defined precisely enough to resolve this apparent contradiction.

The paper overstates its unified-model implications. Language modeling loss is explicitly removed, and no language understanding or generation capability is evaluated. Consequently, sharing an LLM-style architecture and vocabulary does not demonstrate a functioning unified multimodal model.

Claims about efficiency are incomplete. Saying that training used 48 GPUs is not meaningful without training time or total accelerator-hours, and parameter comparisons apparently omit the adopted pretrained Cosmos visual tokenizer.

The societal-impact discussion proposes future safeguards but does not document safeguards actually applied to the released model or training corpus. Provenance, consent, copyright, privacy, demographic bias, and harmful-content filtering for the large undisclosed dataset remain unaddressed.

The empirical results are competitive for the model and data scale: the 3.6B model matches or approaches substantially larger systems on GenEval and VBench-I2V and remains competitive on VBench-T2V without a large external text encoder.

The paper provides useful diagnostic experiments for the proposed design choices, including comparisons among 1D RoPE, M-RoPE, and MM-RoPE; ablations of distributed frequency allocation and coordinate scaling; frame-wise loss analysis; inference-mask sensitivity; and latency measurements.

The framing is practically relevant: retaining a standard Llama-style backbone, using a shared discrete vocabulary, and training on 48 GPUs suggest a comparatively accessible route toward autoregressive image and video generation.
The presentation is generally clear, with informative algorithms, equations, visualizations, architectural details, limitations, and a discussion of societal risks and possible safeguards.
weaknesses: The evidence for the main components is weaker than the headline benchmark results. Most MM-RoPE ablations report validation loss from a 0.5B model rather than generation metrics or human judgments, while AR-DF lacks a complete quantitative comparison against random masking and independent diffusion forcing on standard video benchmarks.

The training objective is described inconsistently: equations define M as selecting visible tokens, but the text states that cross-entropy is computed only on the unmasked tokens. That would encourage trivial copying and conflict with masked-token generation. The exact loss mask must be clarified, ideally with a formal equation.

The unified-model positioning is overstated. The system removes language next-token loss and evaluates neither language modeling nor multimodal understanding, so the experiments establish compatibility with an LLM-style architecture rather than preservation of, or progress toward, a genuinely unified understanding-and-generation model.

GenEval captions are rewritten using Qwen-32B, whereas the reported baseline numbers may use the benchmark's original prompts. This potentially confounds the comparison and should be supplemented with results on unmodified prompts and controlled prompt-rewriting baselines.

Video evaluation is limited to selected VBench columns and a small number of qualitative frame strips. Full benchmark reporting, human preference studies, temporal or physics-focused metrics, and direct evaluation of longer generation would make the video-quality claims substantially more convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claimed efficiency: the paper does not adequately document dataset sources and filtering, recaptioning details, stage lengths, total optimization steps or compute, sampling hyperparameters, or data licensing. The code-and-model statement also lacks an accessible link in the submitted manuscript.

MM-RoPE is a relatively incremental modification of existing multidimensional RoPE schemes, and temporal tube masking is an established masking pattern. The novelty therefore lies primarily in their adaptation and combination, making strong experimental validation especially important.
